extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/economic theory (readers of classical social theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the defining features, motives, and evidences of a leisure class as presented in Veblen's The Theory of the Leisure Class. Focuses on social markers (leisure, consumption, manners, insignia) and the motives behind accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth as honorific evidence / basis of reputability
rubrics_metrics.description: The possession of wealth confers honour and becomes the conventional basis of reputability and self-respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth initially valued as evidence of prowess/trophy, later comes to be intrinsically honourable; possession of goods becomes necessary for a reputable standing and self-complacency. Wealth transmitted by inheritance can be even more honorific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary emulation as primary motive for accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The root motive of ownership and accumulation is emulation — a desire to excel others in pecuniary standing (an invidious comparison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulation is driven more by desire for esteem and relative ranking than by subsistence or physical comfort; this motive persists across stages of development and makes satiation impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous leisure (abstention from productive work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstention from productive labour is the conventional and honorific mark of superior pecuniary achievement; leisure is non-productive consumption of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labour is associated with weakness/subjection and therefore dishonourable; conspicuous abstention from labour is required to display pecuniary strength, especially in predatory/quasi-peaceable stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupations qualifying as leisure-class activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable occupations for the leisure class are government, war, sports, devout observances, and the chase as sport — activities ostensible not for productive gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities are treated as meritorious because they evidence non-productive time or exploitative (honourable-seeming) achievement rather than productive labour; hunting split into trade (productive) vs sport (leisure/exploit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous display — leisure must be evidenced publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth and leisure must be put in evidence to earn esteem; public display and visible signs are necessary for reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be direct (visible ease, servants) or indirect (tangible lasting results of private leisure); esteem is awarded only on evidence, so the leisure-class member must exhibit signs of unproductivity to spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lasting evidence of private leisure (tangible and intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private leisure should leave tangible or immaterial markers (trophies, products of others' labour, badges) that attest to the leisure spent out of public view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible evidence: trophies, booty, material products. Immaterial evidence: quasi-scholarly or quasi-artistic accomplishments (dead languages, household arts, knowledge of dress) and formalized insignia (titles, medals, heraldry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immaterial accomplishments as criteria of leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge and accomplishments that do not directly further human subsistence (languages, syntax, prosody, household arts, knowledge of dress, breeding of fancy animals) serve as recognized evidence of unproductive time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These branches of learning and skill survived because they function as conventional proofs that time was spent in non-productive pursuits; they act as admissible signs of leisure-class culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners, breeding, and decorum as imperative evidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial observances, manners, polite usage, decorum, and formal ceremonies are obtrusive and imperative signs of leisure and status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners tend to flourish under regimes of status and leisure; a refined ceremonial code is treated as a product and exponent of leisure-class life, enforced more during stages when conspicuous leisure is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trophies, insignia, ranks as conventional marks of exploit and status
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of badges of honour (heraldic devices, medals, titles) develop as conventional symbols indicating the amount/degree of exploit or leisure and serve to mark social standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As societies elaborate, trophies evolve into a system of rank and insignia; these are economic/social instruments for communicating past exploit or the fact of leisure to observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabu on labour and moral incompatibility with noble status
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescriptive taboo deems manual, menial labour morally incompatible with the worthy life of the noble or gentleman; in strong instances it overrides self-preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taboo can produce a 'spurious' leisure class — abjectly poor persons who refuse gainful work due to moralized shame attached to labour; historical examples (Polynesian chiefs, a king of France) illustrate extreme adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between consumption for comfort and consumption as status
rubrics_metrics.description: While consumption may serve physical comfort or higher wants, the incentive to accumulate is not primarily consumption but the status conferred by owning wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumption for comfort is present but secondary; pecuniary emulation shapes what is consumed and how, but accumulation's end is ranking and reputability rather than satiation of wants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership's social genesis: from trophies to property in goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Private ownership originates in appropriation (seizure of captives, trophies) and extends from ownership of persons (women, slaves) to ownership of products of their industry and things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early ownership functions as visible evidence of prowess; as societies settle, property consolidates, changing the point of invidious comparison from external enemies to other members of the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invidious comparison and unsatisfiable desire for relative superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: An invidious comparison—rating persons by relative worth—drives continual dissatisfaction and restless striving to outrank others; distribution of wealth cannot satisfy this motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the aim is to excel others, any increase in absolute wealth does not satiate the emulative need; social standards keep resetting, producing perpetual striving for greater pecuniary interval relative to peers.
